newsitem.title: HAITI: Haitian capital paralyzed by anti-government strike.
newsitem.headline: Haitian capital paralyzed by anti-government strike.

text.p: A general strike paralysed much of Haiti on Thursday and sparked random violence from demonstrators who threw rocks, burned tires and smashed windows.
One person who apparently tried to steal food from a World Food Programme warehouse in Cap Haitien was shot and killed by a security guard during the strike.

The protest, called by dozens of organisations, demanded the resignation of Prime Minister Rosny Smarth and demonstrated against tough tactics used by the Haitian National Police to break up a peaceful demonstration last week.
In that demonstration, one man's hand was blown off and many people were trampled after police used explosive tear gas canisters to disperse the crowd.

Regarding the unidentified man who was killed in Cap Haitien, U.N. spokesman Eric Falt said, "We cannot say for sure if this was directly related to the general strike, but possibly to the general strike atmosphere."
Streets throughout the capital were also blocked by burning tires and transportation was difficult even without the support of transportation unions. Many businesses were closed.
Reporters from Radio Kiskeya narrowly escaped after a mob attacked them in Cite Soleil, a sprawling slum outside the capital that was filled with gunshots and black smoke from burning tires all day.

A mob attacked reporters' jeep with rocks, smashing all of the windows. The passengers were forced to run, with the attackers shooting at them with pistols and chasing them, according to reporter Toussaint Gabriel.
Associated Press photographer Daniel Morel and freelancer Shawn Thew were also attacked in the area by a group who stole their cameras.
Strike leaders claimed they were supported by members of more than 160 popular organisations. And independent Radio Metropole reported the strike was observed around the country.
"Anyone who wants to go to work because they need money should think about how much it costs to buy a new windscreen," one strike supporter threatened a motorist in the capital.
Gangs of young men threw rocks at cars in the working class Carrefour-Feuilles section of Port-au-Prince before police broke them up, making some arrests, witnesses said.
The strike was the latest manifestation of growing desperation in a country where unemployment rages as high as 80 percent and the average yearly income is $250, the lowest in the hemisphere.
President Rene Preval has been in office nearly a year and many Haitians say they are frustrated with his government's failure to effect any improvement.
U.N. officials attributed the many closed businesses to intimidation, rather than popular support for the strikers.
